newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Desperate Albanians pray for return of money.
newsitem.headline: Desperate Albanians pray for return of money.

text.p: Albania's pyramid savings scheme bubble has burst and thousands of people across the Balkan state who face financial ruin are asking just one question -- "Will we get our money back?"

When 38-year-old Vali sold her apartment to raise cash for pyramid funds, she thought she was on to a certain winner. Within a year she expected to double her money, but now the investment schemes have crashed and she has nothing.
"Selling flats to get cash for the pyramids became a way of life here," the mother of two said. "All we wanted was to enjoy a Western lifestyle but now we've lost everything."

Fury over the dramatic collapse of some of the most popular schemes unleashed a wave of riots last weekend with many people blaming the government for not protecting them from the risky ventures which have been operating since the early 1990s.
"The government should have warned us that the schemes were dangerous at least a year ago," Vali complained.
President Sali Berisha said the government did all it could to alert people to the problem and said the crash was one of the downsides of a free market economy in a young democracy.

But this will be a hard lesson to learn in this former Stalinist stronghold, as people struggle to come to terms with the birth of free enterprise. Two men in western Albania have already committed suicide in despair and chemists in Tirana report a boom in the sale of tranquilisers.
As the full impact of the financial crisis hits home, people are struggling to adjust to a life without the regular high interest payments which made the pyramids so attractive.

"I might have to sleep in my shop at the end of February because I won't have the money for my apartment rent," said Shpresa, owner of a small kiosk in the centre of Tirana who sold his flat for $13,000 to invest in pyramids.
Albania, Europe's poorest country, has battled to improve living standards since the fall of communism in 1990.

Many saw the high-yielding pyramids as the only way to get rich quickly, and in the early days some people made a fortune. Cars, until recently a rarity in Tirana, now snarl the city's dusty roads and scores of new bars have sprung up.

But by the end of last year, almost every family in the country was believed to have invested in the schemes, with over $1.0 billion tied up in the funds. The system was saturated and it inevitably started to crumble.

Berisha has promised that investors from two of the failed funds, which have had their bank assets seized, will get some of their money back, but suggested that this might come in the form of bank certificates rather than hard cash.
But that idea was unlikely to satisfy people in a country little used to the world of high finance.

"I do not trust the government and if I'm not given cash in hand I won't be happy," said Vali, who now lives in a tiny one-room flat with her husband and two sons. Investors in other failed funds risk getting nothing.

Vali's friend Alma said her family was already feeling the pinch. "People still have some money in their pockets but just you wait and see. I have already cut back on buying meat and rationed my family to just one tangerine per person after lunch, no more," she said.
Landi, a photographer from the southern town of Lushnje, said he could hardly support his three daughters and unemployed wife with his salary.
"All anyone wants to talk about are the schemes. I'm bored of it all, but where can I go?" he said. "We just pray every night that our money comes back home."
